title: ASUS TUF Gaming VG249QE5A: A 146 Hz IPS Monitor With Speakers for Budget Esports
summary: The ASUS TUF Gaming VG249QE5A is a 23.8-inch 1080p IPS monitor that ASUS rates at 146 Hz, 1 ms MPRT and 125% sRGB, with ELMB Sync, 2 W stereo speakers and a headphone jack. It is not the fastest monitor at its price — 180 Hz rivals like the Xiaomi G24i exist — and the stand only tilts. Here is what the specs mean in practice and who should buy it.
description:
## Who is it for?

- Players upgrading from a 60/75 Hz monitor who want a familiar brand and simple setup.
- Budget esports players (Valorant, CS2, Apex) whose PC runs around 100–146 fps at 1080p.
- Small desks where one screen does work, video calls and gaming — and built-in speakers save space.

## Why consider it?

- 146 Hz IPS with Adaptive-Sync and ELMB Sync (ASUS).
- Wide color on paper: 125% sRGB / 90% DCI-P3, 300 nits, 1500:1 (ASUS).
- DisplayPort 1.2 + HDMI 2.0, 2 W × 2 speakers, headphone jack and VESA 100 (ASUS).

specs.value: Up to 146 Hz (ASUS calls it overclocked above 144 Hz); 48–146 Hz range on both DisplayPort and HDMI (ASUS)

sections.title: What is the ASUS TUF Gaming VG249QE5A?
sections.content:
The VG249QE5A is one of the cheapest monitors in ASUS's TUF Gaming range, the brand's value-oriented gaming line. ASUS lists a **23.8-inch IPS panel at 1920 × 1080**, a maximum refresh rate of **146 Hz** (ASUS describes it as an overclock above 144 Hz), 1 ms MPRT, 125% sRGB coverage and a pair of 2 W speakers. It started appearing at US retailers around mid-2025.

It sits in a crowded class. At similar money you can buy 180 Hz IPS monitors such as the Xiaomi G24i, and ASUS itself sells a faster sibling, the VG249QM5A, listed by US retailers as a 240 Hz model. The VG249QE5A's pitch is not raw speed but a balanced package: a major brand, wide color, speakers and a headphone jack, and simple plug-and-play setup.

sections.title: Picture quality: wide color on paper, but use the sRGB mode
sections.content:
ASUS rates the panel at **300 cd/m²**, **1500:1** typical contrast and **125% sRGB / 90% DCI-P3** coverage. Those are strong numbers for a budget IPS monitor — the Xiaomi G24i, for comparison, is rated at 250 nits and 1000:1. Vietnamese retailer Phong Vu, which used the monitor for its blog review, found colors vivid in games and viewing angles wide, with a little IPS glow in the corners of dark scenes in a dim room.

The catch with a gamut wider than sRGB is oversaturation: most games, websites and videos are mastered for sRGB, so a 125% sRGB panel can make skin tones and reds look too punchy. If you want natural color, pick the sRGB or a calibrated GameVisual mode rather than the default. And at 1080p on 23.8 inches (about 93 pixels per inch), text is acceptable for office work but noticeably softer than on a 27-inch 1440p screen.

What it **doesn't** have: ASUS's spec sheet lists **no HDR certification**. Phong Vu describes the HDR experience as basic. Don't buy it for HDR movies or games.

sections.title: Gaming: what 146 Hz, 1 ms MPRT and ELMB Sync really mean
sections.content:
Going from 60 or 75 Hz to 146 Hz is the big upgrade here — motion is far smoother and easier to track in shooters. The jump from 146 Hz to 180 Hz (the Xiaomi G24i) is much smaller and mostly matters if your PC actually delivers more than 146 fps in your games. Many budget PCs running modern shooters at 1080p land around 100–150 fps, which is exactly where a 146 Hz panel makes sense.

Two spec details are easy to misread. First, **1 ms MPRT is not 1 ms pixel response**: MPRT measures perceived motion blur and is usually achieved with backlight strobing (ASUS's ELMB), so it isn't comparable with the 1 ms GTG figure other brands quote. ASUS does not publish a GTG figure for this model, and no independent lab measurement of its pixel response could be found. Second, **ELMB Sync** lets you use strobing and Adaptive-Sync together; strobing dims the image and works best at high, stable frame rates — Phong Vu reports it looked best above about 85 fps.

ASUS lists the 48–146 Hz range on both DisplayPort and HDMI, so the included HDMI cable can drive the full refresh rate. Shadow Boost (brightens dark areas) and Dynamic Crosshair (an on-screen crosshair overlay) are extras; crosshair overlays may be frowned upon in some competitive settings.

sections.title: Stand, ports and speakers: practical, but basic
sections.content:
The stand **only tilts** (+23° to −5° per ASUS) — no height, swivel or pivot adjustment. That is common at this price, but if you're tall, use a laptop next to it or sit close, you may end up stacking it on books. It has a **VESA 100 × 100** mount, so a budget gas-spring arm like the North Bayou F80 (which supports VESA 75 and 100) can fix the ergonomics.

Ports are minimal: **one DisplayPort 1.2 and one HDMI 2.0**, plus an earphone jack. There is **no USB-C**, no USB hub and only one HDMI input, so connecting both a PC and a console means swapping cables or using DisplayPort for the PC. Note that Phong Vu's review says there is no 3.5 mm jack, but ASUS's official spec sheet lists one — trust the spec sheet but check the back panel photo of the unit you buy.

The **2 W × 2 speakers** are the VG249QE5A's practical advantage over the Xiaomi G24i, which has none. Expect them to be fine for video calls, YouTube and system sounds, not for games or music — Phong Vu rates them average. The power supply is internal, so there's no external power brick on the desk.

sections.title: VG249QE5A vs Xiaomi G24i vs VSP IP2705F — and similar ASUS names
sections.content:
We've covered three budget monitors on this site; here's how they line up on paper:

- **ASUS VG249QE5A** (this review): 23.8-inch IPS, 146 Hz, 300 nits, 125% sRGB, DP 1.2 + HDMI 2.0, speakers, VESA 100, internal power. The most rounded package.
- **Xiaomi Gaming Monitor G24i**: 23.8-inch Fast IPS, 180 Hz, 1 ms GTG (Xiaomi lab), 250 nits, 99% sRGB with factory calibration, DP 1.4 + HDMI 2.0, **no speakers**, VESA 75, external adapter. Better for high-fps esports, dimmer and fewer extras.
- **VSP IP2705F**: 27-inch IPS at 1080p, 100 or 120 Hz depending on the listing, HDMI 1.4 + VGA only, speakers. A bigger screen for less money, but softer text and no DisplayPort — and it's sold mainly in Vietnam.

Be careful with similar ASUS model codes. The VG249QM5A is a faster 240 Hz model at a higher price; the older VG249Q1A is a different, earlier TUF monitor. Some retailer titles also round the VG249QE5A down to 144 Hz — it's the same monitor.

sections.title: Who should buy it — and who shouldn't
sections.content:
**Buy it if you:**
- Are upgrading from 60/75 Hz and want a smooth, colorful 1080p IPS monitor from a major brand.
- Play esports titles on a mid-range PC that runs roughly 100–146 fps.
- Want built-in speakers and a headphone jack on a small desk.
- Plan to add a VESA 100 monitor arm later.

**Skip it if you:**
- Have a PC that easily exceeds 180 fps in your main game — a 180 Hz Xiaomi G24i or a 240 Hz model makes more of it.
- Need height adjustment out of the box, USB-C or more than one HDMI port.
- Want real HDR, or sharp text for spreadsheets and coding (look at 27-inch 1440p instead).
- Care most about accurate sRGB color without fiddling with picture modes.

sections.title: Sources for this review
sections.content: Zero Technology **has not used** the ASUS TUF Gaming VG249QE5A. This review is compiled and analyzed from: ASUS's official product and tech-spec pages (panel, refresh range, MPRT, color gamut, ports, stand, power, accessories); Vietnamese retailer Phong Vu's hands-on blog review (impressions of color, IPS glow, ELMB Sync, speakers); and ASUS's Canadian eShop (regular price). No independent lab review was found (RTINGS, Monitors Unboxed, Tom's Hardware) of this exact model, so response time and real brightness are unverified. Phong Vu's review disagrees with ASUS on the headphone jack and tilt range; ASUS's figures are used here. Updated November 2026. Images are official ASUS product images.

sections.title: Should you buy the ASUS TUF Gaming VG249QE5A?
sections.content: Yes, if you want a well-rounded first high-refresh monitor and value the brand, speakers and wide color more than the last few hertz. Its 146 Hz is enough for most budget PCs, ASUS's specs are good on paper and it's easy to set up with the included HDMI cable. The trade-offs are a tilt-only stand, no HDR, minimal ports and the lack of independent lab tests. **Buy it on sale** — discounted, it's a sensible pick; at full price, the 180 Hz Xiaomi G24i is the faster alternative if you don't need speakers.

pros: 146 Hz IPS with Adaptive-Sync and ELMB Sync — a large step up from 60/75 Hz (ASUS).
Strong on-paper picture specs for the price: 300 nits, 1500:1, 125% sRGB / 90% DCI-P3 (ASUS).
Built-in 2 W × 2 speakers and an earphone jack — the Xiaomi G24i has no speakers.
Full 146 Hz over both DisplayPort 1.2 and HDMI 2.0, and an HDMI cable is included.
Internal power supply and VESA 100 mount for standard monitor arms.
Widely sold from a major brand and often discounted below its regular price.
cons: Tilt-only stand: no height, swivel or pivot adjustment.
146 Hz is slower than 180 Hz rivals like the Xiaomi G24i at a similar price.
1 ms MPRT isn't a pixel-response figure; ASUS lists no GTG number and no independent lab test was found.
No HDR certification, and the wide gamut can oversaturate sRGB content unless you switch modes.
Only one DisplayPort and one HDMI input; no USB-C or USB hub.
Speakers are only adequate for calls and video.
buying_advice: A sensible first high-refresh monitor if you want speakers, wide color and a major brand — best bought on sale. For high-fps esports without speakers, the 180 Hz Xiaomi G24i is the faster choice.

faq.question: Is the VG249QE5A good for FPS games?
faq.answer: Yes. 146 Hz with Adaptive-Sync is a big improvement over 60/75 Hz and suits Valorant, CS2 or Apex on a PC running around 100–146 fps. If your PC regularly exceeds 180 fps, a faster monitor uses that headroom better.

faq.question: Is 146 Hz really different from 144 Hz?
faq.answer: Not noticeably — 2 Hz is marketing. ASUS calls it an overclock above 144 Hz, and some retailers list it as 144 Hz. It's the same monitor either way.

faq.question: Does it support HDR?
faq.answer: ASUS's spec sheet lists no HDR certification, and Phong Vu describes HDR as basic. Don't buy it for HDR content.

faq.question: Can I adjust the height?
faq.answer: No, the stand only tilts (+23° to −5°). Use the VESA 100 × 100 mount with a monitor arm such as the North Bayou F80 for height and swivel.

faq.question: VG249QE5A or Xiaomi G24i?
faq.answer: Choose the ASUS for speakers, a headphone jack, higher rated brightness (300 vs 250 nits), internal power and VESA 100. Choose the Xiaomi G24i for 180 Hz, a 1 ms GTG rating and factory calibration — but it has no speakers and a smaller VESA 75 mount.

faq.question: Does it work with PS5 or Xbox?
faq.answer: Yes, over HDMI 2.0 at 1080p. Consoles top out at 120 Hz, so the 146 Hz maximum mainly benefits PC. There's only one HDMI port, so a PC plus console setup needs the PC on DisplayPort.
